name: Aranmula Kannadi (Aranmula metal mirror) craft community
tagline: The secret metal mirror craft of Aranmula — living heritage and temple tradition
summary: A small community of artisan families in Aranmula, Pathanamthitta, handcraft the unique Aranmula Kannadi—front‑surface metal mirrors made to a secret alloy recipe and GI‑protected.
description: Aranmula Kannadi is a rare front‑surface metal mirror made by a handful of traditional artisan (Vishwakarma/Viswabrahmana) families in Aranmula village, Pathanamthitta. The mirrors are polished on the front so they reflect without glass or silvering.

The craft links closely to the Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple and local river festivals; the alloy recipe and polishing techniques remain community knowledge passed down within families. The product has a Geographical Indication (GI) registration (2004–05).
Visitors to Aranmula can watch artisans at small workshops, buy certified mirrors and hear the village stories that connect the craft to temple ritual and the famous Vallamkali (boat‑race) tradition.

Because production is small and specialised, authenticity matters: genuine mirrors carry community certification markings introduced in recent years; confirm provenance and buy from recognised artisans or authorised outlets.
highlights: Unique front‑surface metal mirror (no glass) with exceptional clarity
Made by a very small community of artisan families in Aranmula
Workshops and small family‑run centres in and near Aranmula (buy locally for authenticity)
Linked to Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple and river festivals (Vallamkali)
International visibility — included in recent international exhibitions

sections.heading: Background
body: Aranmula’s metal mirror tradition is centuries old and passed down inside specialist Vishwakarma/Viswabrahmana families. The mirrors are produced from a secret alloy and a labour‑intensive polishing process that produces a front‑surface reflection, unlike ordinary glass mirrors.

The Aranmula Kannadi holds ritual and cultural significance locally — historically used for deity viewing and considered auspicious in households. The craft received Geographical Indication protection in 2004–05 to safeguard its identity and local makers.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Visit small family workshops and authorised handicraft outlets in Aranmula and nearby Malakkara or Edayaranmula to watch casting, finishing and the final hand‑polishing stages. Artisans often explain motifs and frame designs; workshops are small and visits are best during daytime.

Combine a mirror visit with the Parthasarathy Temple precinct and, if your travel dates match, the Aranmula Vallamkali (boat race) and temple festivals. Buy mirrors directly from makers or DTPC/authorised outlets to ensure authenticity and ask for provenance details.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Getting there: Aranmula is a temple village in Pathanamthitta district. The nearest railway station is Chengannur (about 9–11 km); the nearest major airport commonly used is Trivandrum International Airport (about 117 km by road). Reach Aranmula by road from Pathanamthitta and Chengannur; local buses and taxis serve the village.

Best time and access: The dry, comfortable season is October–March; the Onam season (August–September) is important for local river pageantry (Uthrattathi Vallamkali) but dates move with the Malayalam calendar — check current festival dates before you go. Workshops may be affected by local festival rituals or temple schedules, so confirm opening times before travel.

latest.text: An Aranmula mirror was included in the Rijksmuseum exhibition 'Asian Bronze. 4000 Years of Beauty' (27 Sep 2024 – 12 Jan 2025), raising international visibility for the living craft.

A parliamentary committee report (Rajya Sabha/Parliament sources) recommends financial assistance to Aranmula Kannadi artisans and suggests steps towards recognition and conservation, including consideration for inscription and support.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (dry season); Onam (Aug–Sep) for boat‑race events — confirm festival dates.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Nearest railhead Chengannur (≈9–11 km). Nearest major airport commonly used: Trivandrum International Airport (≈117 km). Road access via Pathanamthitta or Chengannur; local buses and taxis connect Aranmula village and heritage sites.
etiquette: Buy from recognised artisan workshops or authorised outlets — ask for provenance; many genuine mirrors carry community authentication markings introduced in recent years (check for the maker’s mark/hologram and certificate).
Mirrors are handcrafted and made to order; expect lead times and handle pieces carefully — confirm shipping/packaging before purchase.
Respect temple etiquette at Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple (dress and photography rules) when combining a craft visit with temple sightseeing.
Ask artisans about their process and history — direct support (buying or commissioning work) helps sustain the community; confirm prices and delivery details before payment.
